source.title: Open problems posed at the eighth international conference on fuzzy set theory and applications

accepted.question_text: For a strict triangular norm T on [0, 1], let F_T be the smallest class of functions from [0, 1] to [0, 1] that contains the identity function and is closed under T, under the standard negation n(x) = 1 - x, and under limits of comonotone sequences. Let T_P be the product t-norm, for which F_TP is the class of all Borel measurable functions from [0, 1] to [0, 1]. Let T_H be the Hamacher product T_H(x, y) = xy / (x + y - xy) for (x, y) not equal to (0, 0), and call a strict t-norm nearly Hamacher when it is isomorphic to T_H by an isomorphism that also generates the standard negation. Does there exist a strict t-norm T such that F_T is different from both F_TP and F_TH? If F_T equals F_TH for a strict t-norm T, must T be nearly Hamacher?

evidence.quote: A triangular norm (t-norm for short) T : [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] is an associative, commutative, non-decreasing function such that 1 acts as a neutral element.

For a strict t-norm T let F_T be the smallest set of all functions from [0, 1] to [0, 1] containing the identity function and being closed under T, the standard negation n given by n(x) = 1 - x, and under limits of comonotone sequences.
Problem 2.1. Is there a strict t-norm T such that F_T != F_TP and F_T != F_TH? If F_T = F_TH for some strict t-norm T, is T then necessarily nearly Hamacher?

accepted.question_text: A triangular norm, or t-norm, is an associative, commutative, non-decreasing function T: [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] with 1 as a neutral element. For p in (1, infinity), characterize all t-norms that are 1-Lipschitz with respect to the L_p norm; more generally, characterize all t-norms that are k-Lipschitz with respect to the L_p norm for a given k >= 1.

evidence.quote: A triangular norm (t-norm for short) T : [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] is an associative, commutative, non-decreasing function such that 1 acts as a neutral element.
Problem 3.1. Characterize all t-norms which are 1-Lipschitz (or, generally, k-Lipschitz with k >= 1) with respect to the L_p-norm for p in ]1, infinity[.

accepted.question_text: Is the following characterization true: an Archimedean triangular norm T is 1-Lipschitz with respect to the L_p norm if and only if every additive generator of T is the p-th power of a convex function?

evidence.quote: Each continuous Archimedean t-norm T can be represented by means of a continuous additive generator.
Conjecture 3.2. An Archimedean t-norm T is 1-Lipschitz with respect to the L_p-norm if and only if each of its additive generators is a p-power of a convex function.

accepted.question_text: Let I_n = {0, 1/n, 2/n, ..., 1}. Given any discrete t-norm T on I_n, extend it to a t-norm T* on [0, 1] by setting T*(x, y) = min(x, y) when max{x, y} = 1 and otherwise T*(x, y) = T(floor(nx)/n, floor(ny)/n). Let tau*_n be the set of all such extensions of all discrete t-norms on I_n, and let tau* be the union of tau*_n over all positive integers n. What is the closure of tau* in the norm of uniform convergence? In particular, does that closure contain all strict t-norms, all continuous t-norms, and all t-norms?

evidence.quote: Given a discrete t-norm T on the set I_n = {0, 1/n, 2/n, ..., 1}, one can extend it to a t-norm on [0, 1] by a piecewise constant extension.
Denote tau*_n the set of all such extensions of all discrete t-norms on I_n and put tau* = union over n in N of tau*_n.

Problem 4.1. What is the closure of the set tau* with respect to the norm of uniform convergence? In particular, are the sets of all strict t-norms, of all continuous t-norms and of all t-norms inside?

accepted.question_text: An interval semigroup is a linearly ordered semigroup S = ([0, 1], *, <=) with 0 as annihilator and no neutral element, considered here in the continuous Archimedean case. A non-decreasing mapping f: [0, 1] -> R is a multiplicative generator of S when x * y = f^(-1)(f(x) * f(y)) for all x, y in [0, 1], where f^(-1) denotes the pseudo-inverse of f. Which nilpotent interval semigroups admit a continuous multiplicative generator?

evidence.quote: Such an algebraic structure will be called an interval semigroup: in the sequel, it is intended that S is a continuous Archimedean interval semigroup.
We say that a non-decreasing mapping f : I -> R is a multiplicative generator of S if x * y = f^(-1)(f(x) * f(y)) for all x, y in I.
Problem 5.2. Characterize the nilpotent interval semigroups which admit a continuous multiplicative generator.

accepted.question_text: For continuous Archimedean interval semigroups S = ([0, 1], *, <=) with 0 as annihilator and no neutral element, and with multiplicative generators f satisfying x * y = f^(-1)(f(x) * f(y)), which nilpotent interval semigroups admit only non-continuous multiplicative generators and no continuous multiplicative generator?

evidence.quote: Such an algebraic structure will be called an interval semigroup: in the sequel, it is intended that S is a continuous Archimedean interval semigroup.
Problem 5.3. Characterize the nilpotent interval semigroups which exclusively admit non continuous multiplicative generators.

accepted.question_text: For continuous Archimedean interval semigroups S = ([0, 1], *, <=) with 0 as annihilator and no neutral element, which non-nilpotent interval semigroups do not admit any multiplicative generator f: [0, 1] -> R satisfying x * y = f^(-1)(f(x) * f(y))?

evidence.quote: We say that a non-decreasing mapping f : I -> R is a multiplicative generator of S if x * y = f^(-1)(f(x) * f(y)) for all x, y in I.
Problem 5.4. Characterize the non nilpotent interval semigroups which do not admit any multiplicative generator.

accepted.question_text: A 3-copula C has three marginal 2-copulas C12(x, y) = C(x, y, 1), C23(y, z) = C(1, y, z), and C13(x, z) = C(x, 1, z). A triple (C12, C23, C13) obtained this way is called compatible. Given a triple (C, D, E) of 2-copulas, characterize exactly when it is compatible. Also, for a fixed 2-copula E, determine all pairs (C, D) for which (C, D, E) is compatible, and for fixed 2-copulas C and D, determine all 2-copulas E for which (C, D, E) is compatible.

evidence.quote: A (two-dimensional) copula is a function C : [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] such that C(0, x) = C(x, 0) = 0 and C(1, x) = C(x, 1) = x for all x in [0, 1].
Each 3-copula C induces three marginal 2-copulas C12, C23, and C13 given by C12(x, y) = C(x, y, 1), C23(y, z) = C(1, y, z), and C13(x, z) = C(x, 1, z).
For a given triplet of 2-copulas (C, D, E), find a characterization ensuring its compatibility.

accepted.question_text: Archimedean copulas are copulas generated by additive generators. For dimension 2, every associative 2-copula C: [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] with C(x, x) < x for all x in (0, 1) is Archimedean. Is there an algebraic characterization of Archimedean 3-copulas, and more generally of Archimedean n-copulas for n > 2?

evidence.quote: Problem 6.2. Copulas generated by means of additive generators are called Archimedean copulas.
Each associative 2-copula C : [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] is Archimedean whenever C(x, x) < x for all x in ]0, 1[.
Is there an algebraic characterization for Archimedean 3-copulas (or, generally, for n-copulas with n > 2)?

accepted.question_text: Define an n-quasi-copula by keeping the boundary properties of an n-copula and replacing the n-copula volume condition with the 1-Lipschitz condition |Q(x1, ..., xn) - Q(y1, ..., yn)| <= sum_i |xi - yi|. Generated quasi-copulas are called Archimedean quasi-copulas; when n = 2, Archimedean quasi-copulas are necessarily copulas, while n-copulas form a proper subclass of n-quasi-copulas in general. Is there an algebraic characterization of Archimedean 3-quasi-copulas, and more generally of Archimedean n-quasi-copulas for n > 2?

evidence.quote: Replacing property (iii) of copulas by the 1-Lipschitz property ... the class of n-quasi-copulas is defined.
Generated quasi-copulas are called Archimedean quasi-copulas and, for n = 2, Archimedean quasi-copulas are necessarily copulas.
Is there an algebraic characterization for Archimedean 3-quasi-copulas (or, generally, for n-quasi-copulas with n > 2)?

accepted.question_text: Every n-copula C can be represented by measure-preserving transformations phi_i: [0, 1] -> [0, 1] for i = 1, ..., n through C(x1, ..., xn) = lambda(phi_1^{-1}([0, x1]) intersect ... intersect phi_n^{-1}([0, xn])), where lambda is Lebesgue measure on the Borel subsets of [0, 1]. Which particular properties of an n-copula C correspond to representations in which the n transformations are all ergodic, or all weakly mixing?

evidence.quote: Each n-copula C can be represented by means of n measure preserving transformations phi_i: [0, 1] -> [0, 1], i = 1, ..., n.
C(x1, ..., xn) = lambda(phi_1^{-1}([0, x1]) intersect ... intersect phi_n^{-1}([0, xn])).
Are there any particular properties of an n-copula C which are represented by means of n ergodic (or n weakly mixing) transformations?

accepted.question_text: A semicopula, also called a conjunctor, is a non-decreasing mapping S: [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] with neutral element 1, so S(x, 1) = S(1, x) = x for all x in [0, 1]. A quasi-copula is a two-dimensional copula-like function satisfying the stated boundary conditions, componentwise monotonicity, and 1-Lipschitz continuity; every 1-Lipschitz semicopula with respect to the L1 norm is a quasi-copula and is 2-Lipschitz with respect to the Chebyshev norm L_infinity. Characterize all associative semicopulas that are 2-Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity. Characterize all quasi-copulas that are exactly 2-Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity, meaning not Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity for any constant c < 2. More generally, for each c in [1, 2], characterize all quasi-copulas that are exactly c-Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity.

evidence.quote: A mapping S : [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] is called a semicopula (conjunctor) if it is non-decreasing in both coordinates and if 1 is the neutral element of S.
Problem 7.1. Characterize all associative semicopulas which are 2-Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity.
Characterize all quasi-copulas which are exactly 2-Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity, i.e., which are not Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity for any constant c < 2.
For each constant c in [1, 2], characterize all quasi-copulas which are exactly c-Lipschitz with respect to L_infinity.

accepted.question_text: A fuzzy implication is a function I: [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] that is non-increasing in its first component, non-decreasing in its second component, satisfies I(1, 0) = 0, and satisfies I(0, x) = I(x, 1) = 1 for every x in [0, 1]. A t-norm T is an associative, commutative, non-decreasing operation on [0, 1] with neutral element 1. For a given continuous t-norm T, characterize all fuzzy implications I satisfying the law of importation I(x, I(y, z)) = I(T(x, y), z) for all x, y, z in [0, 1]. Since commutativity of T makes this law imply the exchange principle I(x, I(y, z)) = I(y, I(x, z)), does the exchange principle conversely imply the existence of a t-norm T for which the law of importation holds? If so, is T unique; if not, give an example and characterize the fuzzy implications for which the converse is true.

evidence.quote: A function I : [0, 1]^2 -> [0, 1] is called a (fuzzy) implication if it is non-increasing in its first component, non-decreasing in its second component and satisfies I(1, 0) = 0.
For a given (continuous) t-norm T, characterize all fuzzy implications which satisfy the law of importation with respect to T.
Does the exchange principle imply that there exists a t-norm such that the law of importation holds? If yes, is the t-norm uniquely determined?

accepted.question_text: Let a = (a1, ..., an) be a vector of positive real numbers. For a continuous strictly monotone function f: (0, infinity) -> R, define the quasi-arithmetic mean M_f(a) = f^{-1}((1/n) * sum_{k=1}^n f(a_k)). Find all pairs of functions (f, g) and (u, v) for which M_f(a) - M_g(a) <= M_u(a) - M_v(a).

evidence.quote: Let a = (a1, ..., an) be an n-dimensional vector of positive real numbers, n in N.
Consider the quasi-arithmetic mean defined by M_f(a) = f^{-1}(1/n sum f(a_k)), where f : ]0, infinity[ -> R is a continuous and strictly monotone function.
Problem 9.1. Find all pairs (f, g), (u, v) such that M_f(a) - M_g(a) <= M_u(a) - M_v(a).

accepted.question_text: Let p > 0 and 0 < q < infinity. Let w: (0, infinity) -> R be positive and Lebesgue integrable, and define W(x) = integral from 0 to x of w(s) ds. For positive measurable weights u and v, and for a real continuous strictly monotone function g with inverse g^{-1}, define the generalized weighted mean operator of a positive Lebesgue integrable function f by M^g_w f(x) = g^{-1}((1 / W(x)) * integral from 0 to x of w(t) g(f(t)) dt). Find necessary and sufficient conditions on u and v and establish a class of functions g such that the inequality (integral_0^infinity u(x) (M^g_w f(x))^q dx)^(1/q) <= C (integral_0^infinity v(x) f(x)^p dx)^(1/p) holds for every f >= 0 with a positive finite constant C. Also estimate the best possible constant C in this inequality.

evidence.quote: Let p > 0, 0 < q < infinity and define W : ]0, infinity[ -> R by W(x) = integral from 0 to x w(s) ds.
Find necessary and sufficient conditions on the positive measurable functions u, v (weights) and establish a class of functions g.
Estimate the best possible constant C in (2).

accepted.question_text: Let L^+_1([a, b]) be the vector space of positive real Lebesgue integrable functions on [a, b], where a < b. For (p, f) in L^+_1([a, b]) x L^+_1([a, b]), with f: [a, b] -> [alpha, beta], and for a real continuous strictly monotone function phi: [alpha, beta] -> R, define the generalized weighted quasi-arithmetic mean M_[a,b],phi(p, f) = phi^{-1}((1 / ||p||_[a,b]) * integral_a^b p(x) phi(f(x)) dx). Determine all strictly monotone continuous functions phi, psi: [alpha, beta] -> R for which M_[a,b],phi(p, f) + M_[a,b],psi(p, g) = p(a) f(a) + p(b) g(b) holds for every pair of continuous functions f and g on [a, b].

evidence.quote: Let L^+_1([a, b]) be the vector space of all real positive Lebesgue integrable functions on [a, b] with a, b in R and a < b.
The generalized weighted quasi-arithmetic mean M_[a,b],phi(p, f) of a function f with respect to a weight function p is given by M_[a,b],phi(p, f) = phi^{-1}(1/||p|| integral_a^b p(x) phi(f(x)) dx).

Problem 9.3. Determine all those strictly monotone and continuous functions phi, psi : [alpha, beta] -> R for which the equation M_[a,b],phi(p, f) + M_[a,b],psi(p, g) = p(a)f(a) + p(b)g(b) holds for every continuous functions f, g on [a, b].

accepted.question_text: Let A be the set of all symmetric idempotent matrices on the real vector space R^n; that is, for every A in A, AA = A. Let I be the identity matrix and 0 the zero matrix. A fuzzy relation s: A x A -> [0, 1] is an s-map if s(I, I) = 1; if A, B in A satisfy AB = BA = 0 then s(A, B) = 0; and if A, B in A satisfy AB = BA = 0, then for every C in A, s(A + B, C) = s(A, C) + s(B, C) and s(C, A + B) = s(C, A) + s(C, B). Must every such s-map be symmetric, meaning s(A, B) = s(B, A) for all A, B in A?

evidence.quote: Let A be the set of all symmetric matrices defined on the real vector space R^n, such that for each A in A we have AA = A.
A fuzzy relation s : A x A -> [0, 1] is called an s-map if (i) s(I, I) = 1.
Problem 10.1. Is the fuzzy relation s necessarily symmetric, i.e., s(A, B) = s(B, A) for all A, B in A?

accepted.question_text: Characterize all bounded chains that can serve as the carrier set of an MV-algebra. Is the existence of an involution on the bounded chain sufficient for it to be a carrier of an MV-algebra? Is the property of a bounded chain being a carrier of an MV-algebra expressible as a first-order property?

evidence.quote: Problem 11.1. Characterize all bounded chains which are carriers of MV-algebras.
Is it enough to require the existence of an involution of the given chain?
Is the property of a bounded chain to be a carrier of an MV-algebra a first order property?

accepted.question_text: An effect algebra is a partial algebra (E; ⊕, 0, 1) with distinct 0 and 1 and a partially defined binary operation ⊕ satisfying commutativity when a ⊕ b is defined, associativity when one side is defined, the existence for every a in E of a unique b with a ⊕ b = 1, and the condition that if 1 ⊕ a is defined then a = 0. Define a <= b iff there is c in E such that a ⊕ c = b; call E a lattice effect algebra or complete effect algebra when (E, <=) is respectively a lattice or complete lattice. Define a <-> b iff a∨b = a⊕(b⊖(a∧b)), let a block B be a maximal subset of E whose elements are pairwise related by <->, set S(E) = {x in E | x ∧ x' = 0}, B(E) = ⋂{B subset E | B is a block of E}, and C(E) = S(E) ∩ B(E). Describe all lattice effect algebras, and all complete lattice effect algebras, satisfying each of the following properties: C(E) = S(E), C(E) = B(E), and C(E) = S(E) = B(E).
accepted.context_brief: effect algebra sharp, block, and center substructures

evidence.quote: A partial algebra (E; ⊕, 0, 1) is called an effect algebra if 0, 1 are two distinct elements and ⊕ is a partially defined binary operation on E.
If (E, <=) is a lattice (complete lattice) then E is called a lattice effect algebra (complete effect algebra).
Problem 12.1. Describe the family of all lattice (complete) effect algebras with one of the following properties: C(E) = S(E), C(E) = B(E), C(E) = S(E) = B(E).
